On returns, and why we keep getting them wrong

Returns are the part of the business that nobody wants to own. They arrive unannounced, in poor packaging, with missing paperwork and a customer who is already unhappy; they take up space that was planned for something else; and they generate work that never appears in anyone's targets. I have looked at returns processes in perhaps a dozen companies now, and I want to set down some general observations, because the same mistakes come up again and again.

The first mistake is to treat returns as an exception. In practice, for most retailers, returns are a steady and predictable flow, often a tenth or more of outbound volume, and they follow the outbound pattern with a lag of a week or two. You can forecast them; you can staff for them; you can design space for them. Yet almost every site I visit handles returns as though each one were a surprise. The upshot is that returns are processed in whatever space and time happens to be free, which means they are processed slowly, and stock that could be resold sits in a cage for weeks, losing value.

The second mistake is to measure returns by cost alone. Of course returns cost money; but the larger cost is usually the value lost whilst the item waits. A coat returned in October and put back on sale in November is worth far less than the same coat put back on sale in October. When I analyse a returns operation, I always ask how long, on average, a resaleable item takes to get from the dock back into sellable stock. Most sites cannot tell me. Those that can are usually horrified by the answer.

There was a memorable kerfuffle at one site, a few years ago, when we found three pallets of returned winter boots in a back corridor, in May. Nobody knew how they had got there; nobody had been told to process them; and the system showed them as already resold. The kerfuffle that followed was loud and largely unproductive, as these things tend to be, but it did lead to the one change that mattered: the company gave returns a single owner, with a single target, measured in days rather than in cost.

The third mistake is to separate returns from the rest of the building. Returns are often pushed to a far corner, towards the back of the site, on the grounds that they are untidy and should be kept out of the way. I understand the instinct; but in practice it means that every returned item travels further, through more hands, before it reaches its proper place. Whilst it is out of sight, it is also out of mind. A small, well-run returns area close to the main stock, with clear rules for grading, is worth far more than a large, tidy one hidden at the back.

What does a good returns process look like? I would point to four features.

It grades quickly. Every returned item should be graded within a day of arrival: resaleable as it is, resaleable after work, sell elsewhere, or dispose of. The grading should be done by experienced people, because a wrong grade is expensive in either direction; and the rules for grading should be written down, owned and reviewed, not held in one supervisor's head.

It moves resaleable stock first. The most valuable thing a returns team can do is get good stock back on sale, so that should be the first task every morning. The upshot of getting this order right is usually dramatic; I have seen sites halve the value lost to returns simply by changing which pile gets attention first.

It feeds back to the rest of the business. Returns are a rich source of information about product quality, sizing, description and packaging, and most businesses waste it. A short weekly note to the buying team, listing the lines with unusually high returns and the reasons given, costs almost nothing and can save a great deal. I always encourage clients to analyse the reasons customers give, crude as they often are, because the patterns are usually clear enough to act on.

It is honest about disposal. Some returned items cannot be resold, and holding on to them in hope only adds cost. A good process sets a clear rule for when an item is written off, and sticks to it. This is where many sites struggle; nobody likes writing off stock, and so it is kept, and kept, and eventually thrown away anyway, at greater cost. You can't eat your cake and have it too: either the item is worth the space it occupies, or it is not, and the decision should be made once.

I want to say a word about technology, because it comes up in every conversation. There are excellent returns systems available, and some of them are worth the money. But I have never seen a system fix a returns operation on its own. The sites that do returns well have a clear owner, clear rules and a sensible layout; the system helps them do what they already do. The sites that do returns badly tend to buy a system in the hope that it will supply the ownership they lack, and it never does. In practice the order matters: owner first, rules second, layout third, system last.

There is also the question of who pays. Many retailers now charge customers for returns, or restrict free returns to members of a loyalty scheme. I have no strong view on the commercial side, which is outside my field; but I would point out that charging for returns does not reduce the work of processing them, it only changes the mix. Fewer casual returns, perhaps, but a higher share of faulty or damaged items, which are slower to grade and harder to resell. Anyone planning such a change should analyse what it does to the returns team's workload, not just to the revenue line.

Finally, a plea. If you run a site, go and stand in your returns area for an hour. Watch what arrives, how it is graded, where it goes and how long it waits. Ask the people working there what slows them down. The upshot, almost always, is a short list of simple changes that nobody had made because nobody had looked. Returns will never be the glamorous end of the business; but they are a part of it that rewards attention more generously than almost any other, and they are drifting towards a larger share of volume every year.
